idea: Replace random order with a target-similarity filter: (1) drop exact/near duplicates (hash of whitespace-normalised lowercase first 500 chars) and obvious junk (docs under 200 chars, non-ASCII-letter ratio high, or fraction of words found in the target_sample vocabulary < 0.5, which catches scrambled-letter text and code). (2) Train a classifier: TfidfVectorizer(analyzer='char_wb', ngram_range=(2,4), max_features=200k, sublinear_tf=True) on the first 3000 chars of each text, LogisticRegression(C=10) with positives = the 200 target_sample docs (class_weight='balanced') and negatives = a seeded random 4000 pool docs; score all surviving pool docs. Also add a hard bonus for WikiText formatting cues (doc starts with '= ' title line, contains ' @-@ ', ' , ', ' . ' tokenised punctuation). (3) Rank by score, take the top docs until their gpt2 token count (estimate via tiktoken on docs, or len(chars)/4 if time is tight) reaches about 1.0*T; if the clearly-target-like set (score above the midpoint between the mean target-sample cross-validated score and the mean pool score) holds less than T tokens, still fill up to T with the next best-scoring docs rather than cycling unless the target-like set is at least 0.5*T, in which case return only that set (it will be cycled). (4) Shuffle the selected indices with the CURATE_SEED-seeded RNG and return.
why: The target is WikiText-style Wikipedia articles while the pool is half off-domain web text, code, scrambled and duplicated junk, so spending all T tokens on deduplicated, target-like documents should cut bpb far more than any ordering tweak.
outcome: dev 1.9206 against 1.9408 for the best at the time, KEPT as the new best

idea: Add a word-order / damage quality filter and stronger dedup on top of the current pipeline, and never fill with junk. (1) Word-order filter: build a set of lowercase word bigrams (whitespace tokens) from the 200 target_sample docs. For each surviving pool doc, compute over its first 6000 chars (a) bigram coverage = fraction of its adjacent word pairs found in the target bigram set, (b) function-word plausibility = fraction of occurrences of ' the ' followed by a token that is not in {',', '.', 'the', 'of', 'and'}, and (c) fraction of whitespace tokens that are in the target vocabulary. Calibrate thresholds from the target itself: split target_sample in two halves, build bigrams from one half, measure (a)/(b)/(c) on the other half, scale (a) for the half-size set by also measuring pool docs with the same half set, and drop pool docs falling below the 2nd-percentile target value minus a small margin on any of the three. This catches word-shuffled, sentence-spliced and character-corrupted Wikipedia-like docs that the char_wb classifier cannot see. (2) Stronger dedup: besides the first-500-char hash, also dedup on the normalised title line ('= Title =') and on hashes of three 200-char windows taken at 25%, 50% and 75% of the doc; when duplicates collide keep the one with the highest bigram coverage, then the longest. (3) Selection: rank the remaining docs by classifier score + format bonus as now, but only fill up to T with docs above the target-like threshold; if that clean set holds at least 0.3*T tokens return just it (cycled) rather than padding with lower-scoring off-domain docs; otherwise pad as before. Keep the seeded shuffle.
why: The current classifier uses within-word character n-grams and a first-500-char hash, so it cannot detect word-shuffled or spliced wiki-style docs or near-duplicates that differ at the start, and these damaged or repeated docs probably still occupy a large share of the T-token budget.
outcome: dev 1.8142 against 1.9206 for the best at the time, KEPT as the new best

idea: Implement a 'compression-diversity' weight: for each document, calculate the compression ratio (ratio of raw char count to the number of unique words) and use it as a tie-breaker in deduplication and a small multiplier in the final ranking score.
why: Higher word-to-character ratios or lower entropy (redundancy) in content often correlate with structured, high-quality information, and this helps distinguish between dense, information-rich Wikipedia-style entries and repetitive or low-quality fluff that the current classifier might still score highly.
